role: Build record and machine code of bw_old and bw_new, the part A binaries
purpose: run_kernels.sh wrote this file on CRB on 2026-11-13 when it built the binaries bw_old and bw_new: the machine state, the compiler flags, the sha256 values and the objdump text of every kernel function. Part A of the rerun of 2026-11-17 ran these two binaries. So this file shows the exact instructions of the old read kernel and of the new read kernel in part A.

main_flow.step: Lines that start with `##` are notes of run_kernels.sh: the machine state, the compiler, the flags and the end of each step. They are lines 1 to 5, 12, 13 and 437 to 439.
The sha256 block (lines 13 to 22) names the sources and the binaries of the build. Lines 19 and 20 are the values that ra.sh checks before part A of the rerun.

A line of the form `=== bw_new k_read ===` starts the objdump text of one function. An instruction line holds the address in hexadecimal, the instruction name and the operands. Each instruction is 4 bytes long.
To find a loop, look for a branch (`b.hi`, `b.cc`, `b.ne`, `b.gt`) whose target address is lower than its own address. The loop runs from the target to the branch.
The new read kernel is the section `bw_new k_read`: 8 loads per loop pass of 256 bytes, and no other use of the data.
The old read kernel is the section `bw_old k_read`: 4 loads and 8 vector adds per loop pass of 128 bytes.
The hand-written loop asmread is in both binaries with the same instructions: `bw_new k_asmread` at lines 81 to 103, and `bw_old k_asmread` at lines 257 to 279.

The sections `k_write`, `k_copy`, `k_asmwrite` and `k_asmcopy` of both binaries are the write and copy kernels (bw_new: lines 39 to 79 and 105 to 153, bw_old: lines 228 to 255 and 281 to 329). Part A timed them too, each in its own process.
The sections `probe.o` and `chase` show code that the whole-chip test does not run.
The last three lines give the result of the self-test and the load after the timed runs of 2026-11-13.

behavior_notes: This file is from the build of 2026-11-13, not from the rerun. The link to the rerun is a sha256 check: ra.sh started part A only after bw_old and bw_new matched lines 19 and 20 [Ref2]. The three part A records of the rerun show the same two values [Ref9].
The part A result folders of the rerun hold their own file named `probe.txt`, written by ra.sh. That file holds no machine code [Ref9].

The binary files bw_old and bw_new are not in the local folders of this project. So this listing cannot be checked against a local binary. Their sha256 values are known only from records, such as lines 19 and 20 of this file, ra.sh and the part A records of the rerun [Ref2] [Ref9].

Per 256 bytes read, the new read kernel and asmread execute 8 loads and 3 other instructions in 1 loop pass. The old read kernel executes 8 loads and 24 other instructions in 2 loop passes: 16 vector adds, 4 integer adds, 2 compares and 2 branches.

The new read kernel (lines 26 to 36) and asmread (lines 88 to 98) have the same loop: 8 `ldp` loads with the same offsets, one `add`, one `cmp` and one branch. They differ in four points: the register numbers, the operand order of `cmp` with the matching branch condition, the loop address, and the 8 stack instructions that asmread executes outside the loop once per call.

Code outside a loop runs once per call. The benchmark reads the clock before the timed calls and after them [Ref3] [Ref4]. So this code is inside the timed interval. One warm-up call before each timed interval is not timed. In part A one call reads the 256 MiB buffer of a thread: 1,048,576 loop passes in `bw_new k_read` and in `k_asmread`, and 2,097,152 loop passes in `bw_old k_read` [Ref2].

The listing holds only the six kernel functions of each binary. It does not show `pass` and `worker` (the functions that call them) or `main` [Ref1]. The statements of this page about the callers come from the source text [Ref3] [Ref4]. Both sources mark every kernel function `noinline`. This forbids the compiler to merge a kernel into its caller [Ref3] [Ref4].

bw_old and bw_new fill their buffers with different write loops. Each thread does the first write (first touch) to its buffers with the `k_write` of its binary, before its first timed interval. This first write is not timed. In bw_old it is the SVE loop at lines 238 to 241 of this file. In bw_new it is the `stp` loop at lines 43 to 53 [Ref3] [Ref4].

The copy of bandwidth.c in the project folder `tmp/agent-scratch/kernels-2026-11-13` is not the exact text of this build. Its sha256 starts with `f1985072`. Line 15 says `c1406e02`. run_kernels.sh ran again at 18:32:18 UTC of the same day, in the mode `probe` (build, machine code and self-test, no timed runs). The record of that run lists the `f1985072` text, the bw_new value of line 20, and machine code equal to lines 23 to 436 of this file [Ref5]. run_kernels.sh builds bw_new at every run [Ref1]. So both texts give the same bw_new.

The two texts differ in comment lines only. An edit of 2026-11-13 18:32:07 UTC replaced 2 comment lines above `k_read` with the 5 comment lines 178 to 182 of the local text [Ref12]. With this edit reversed, the local text has the sha256 value of the earlier text (c1406e02...). No code line differs.

The rerun also ran the runner program bwx12. This file holds no machine code of bwx12. In the bwx12 listing the functions `k_read`, `k_asmread` and `k_oldread` show the same instruction text as lines 25 to 37, 83 to 103 and 157 to 226 of this file, apart from addresses [Ref8].

`bw_old k_read` holds a stack protector check (lines 159 to 160, 163 to 165, 211 to 212, 215 to 218, 221 and 226). It runs once per call. No flag in line 3 asks for it. Insufficient data: which default setting of this gcc adds it. The output of `gcc -Q --help=common` on CRB would resolve it.
The self-test of line 437 covers the kernels of the new source only: selftest.c includes bandwidth.c, not bandwidth.orig.c [Ref7].

words.def: the Arm reference server under test. It has 128 CPUs.
the two halves of the chip. CPUs 0-63 sit on mesh 0. CPUs 64-127 sit on mesh 1.
our runs use CPUs 0-119 only: 64 threads on mesh 0 plus 56 threads on mesh 1. Each thread reads its own buffer of 256 MiB from memory.
million transfers per second, the unit of memory speed.
the whole-chip read test of 2026-11-17 on CRB, run after the memory speed was lowered from 8000 MT/s to 7200 MT/s.
the inner loop of the benchmark that reads memory. On this page "kernel" means this loop. The operating system kernel is always written "Linux kernel".
portable C code with 16 running sums. Each load is followed by an add. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_old and `oldread` in the runner bwx12.
NEON intrinsics (C functions that map to Arm vector instructions), loads only. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_new and `read` in bwx12.
a hand-written load-only loop. It has the same 8 "ldp q" loads per 256 B as the new read kernel. "ldp q" is the Arm instruction that loads two 16-byte vector registers.
the new read kernel or asmread.
the benchmark and its two binaries of 2026-11-13. bw_old was built from the old source, bw_new from the new source.
later runner programs for the same loops. They print one row per thread. bwx12 is the runner of the 2026-11-15 investigation. bwx11 and bwx are older versions.

a process is one start of a benchmark binary. An interval is one timed measurement inside a process. In part A the round (1 or 2) is the round of the script: round 2 runs the processes in the reverse order.
the 120-thread part of the test of 2026-11-13, repeated with the same two binaries.
the script of 2026-11-13 that built bw_old and bw_new on CRB, wrote this file and ran the timed runs of that day.
the program `selftest` that run_kernels.sh builds from selftest.c and runs after the build. It checks what the six kernels of the new source do to memory [Ref7].
an object file that run_kernels.sh compiled from probe.c. It holds three candidates for the copy kernel. run_kernels.sh did not link it and did not run it [Ref1] [Ref6].
ra.sh is the script that ran part A of the rerun. go.sh is the driver script of the rerun that started ra.sh.
the GNU tool that prints the machine code of a binary as assembly text. Here it printed one function per call, without the raw instruction bytes.
a checksum of 256 bits, printed as 64 hexadecimal digits. Equal values mean equal file content.
one execution of the instructions of a loop, from the loop start to the branch that jumps back.
one execution of a kernel function. In part A one call goes once over the whole 256 MiB buffer of a thread.

a statement of the new source, written `__asm__ volatile("" : : ...)`. Its instruction text is empty. It names the 16 loaded values as inputs in vector registers. gcc must have all 16 values in registers at that point. In `k_read` this keeps gcc from deleting the loads [Ref3].
a load instruction reads bytes from memory into a register. A store instruction writes bytes from a register to memory.
load pair and store pair: one instruction moves two registers. With two `q` registers it moves 32 bytes.
the 64-bit integer registers and the stack pointer. `w2` names the low 32 bits of `x2`.
the 32 vector registers of 128 bits each. `q5` names all 16 bytes of register 5. `d5` names its low 8 bytes. `v5.2d` names the same register taken as two 64-bit numbers.
the 128-bit vector instruction set of 64-bit Arm CPUs.

Scalable Vector Extension, a second vector instruction set of Arm. Its registers are named `z0` to `z31`, and their size depends on the CPU. The registers `p0` to `p15` select the elements that an instruction uses.

a check that the compiler adds to a function. At entry the function copies a guard value to the stack next to its local variables. Before it returns, it compares the copy with the guard value. When they differ, it calls `__stack_chk_fail`.
transparent huge pages: a Linux feature that backs memory with 2 MiB pages without a request of the program.
the first write to a new buffer. Linux assigns the physical memory pages of the buffer at that moment.
the number of tasks that are runnable or wait for disk input and output, averaged by Linux over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes (file /proc/loadavg).

the column pcpu of the tool ps, shown in lines 6 to 11 of this file. It is the CPU time that a process has used, divided by the time since the process started. So it is an average over the life of the process. It is not the use at the moment of the reading.
